blocks.heading: Horizontal integration
blocks.text:
Horizontal integration joins firms at the same stage of production in the same industry. Two invented bakeries combining their businesses provide a straightforward example: both turn ingredients into baked goods. They do not become vertically integrated merely because one is larger or uses a different building. The distinguishing test concerns their place in the production chain and industry, not their geography. A firm opening another outlet by itself is also different from joining an existing separate business, although both can enlarge operations.

Combining similar activities may allow shared facilities, larger purchases or removal of duplicated administration. It may also reduce rivalry between the former competitors. These are potential effects, not part of the definition. The firms may have incompatible systems, different quality routines or locations that limit practical sharing. A larger combined output must have sufficient demand to use its capacity. In an invented bakery merger, cheaper bulk flour might be offset by additional transport between sites. Evaluating the transaction therefore requires more than naming horizontal integration. First classify the relationship, then examine the possible mechanism and its costs. No current merger-law threshold or real named business is needed to make this economic comparison. The question is what activities have been combined and how their resources or market position may change. A joining of similar firms may increase market share, but that possible effect is not the defining test. The classification still depends on stage and industry. If a case supplies no production relationship, ask what each business does before choosing a label rather than using its motive as a substitute.

blocks.heading: Forward vertical integration
blocks.text:
Forward vertical integration joins a firm with an activity at a later stage of the same production chain, towards the customer. An invented juice producer acquiring a shop that sells its juice moves forward. The shop is closer to final consumers than the processing stage. The term does not mean moving to a new town, raising the selling price or simply producing more juice. It describes the ownership or control relationship across stages.

Possible motives include securing an outlet, gaining better information about customers or coordinating availability. The producer may keep some distribution activity within the business rather than relying on an independent retailer. It also takes on retail responsibilities and associated costs. Running a shop requires suitable staff, premises and knowledge, so expertise in production alone does not establish success. Other retailers may respond differently when a supplier becomes a competitor. The outcome depends on capacity, demand and organisation. For classification, keep the focal business explicit: a retailer acquiring a producer is a backward move from the retailer’s position, even though the same stages are connected. This prevents memorising a pair of business names without understanding direction. Explain earlier or later relative to the starting firm and then separately evaluate whether the resulting control or coordination advantage outweighs the new commitments.

blocks.heading: Backward vertical integration
blocks.text:
Backward vertical integration joins a firm with an earlier stage of the same chain, towards its input sources. An invented furniture maker acquiring a timber supplier moves backward. The supplier provides an input before the furniture-production stage. The direction is about the chain, not whether goods physically travel west, inland or back to a warehouse. A furniture maker buying another furniture maker would instead be horizontal because the businesses occupy the same stage.

The motive might be more control over input timing, quality or availability. That can reduce the difficulty of depending on an outside supplier, but internal ownership does not eliminate production risk. The acquired supplier may face weather, equipment or skill constraints. The furniture maker must also manage an activity different from its existing work and commit resources that could have served other purposes. A guarantee of cheaper materials cannot be inferred from ownership alone. A fair evaluation compares the full cost and reliability of internal supply with realistic alternatives. This links to derived factor demand: inputs are wanted because they support the final output. Integration changes who controls the input activity; it does not remove the need for useful contribution or efficient organisation. In a prompt, identify what the focal firm makes and which acquired activity provides its inputs before assigning the backward label.

blocks.heading: Conglomerate integration
blocks.text:
Conglomerate integration joins businesses in unrelated industries or activities. An invented packaging manufacturer combining with an unrelated guesthouse operator illustrates the distinction. The guesthouse is neither another packaging manufacturer nor an earlier or later stage in making the packages. Simply serving customers does not make all businesses part of the same production chain. The classification requires the relationship between the specific activities.

Possible motives include spreading commercial risks or entering a new market. Different demand patterns might reduce dependence on one activity. However, unrelated expertise can be difficult to manage, and the purchase may add complexity without useful shared production resources. Risks may also move together: a broad downturn can affect several activities at once. Diversification does not mean losses become impossible. A combined firm still needs suitable managers, finance and information for its operations. This connects to risk-bearing economies of scale in the next unit, but the integration category alone does not establish an average-cost reduction. An invented firm acquiring an unrelated service could increase its scale and complexity without improving efficiency. State the category first, then examine whether the claimed benefits arise. Across the integration routes, the defining test is same stage, later stage, earlier stage or unrelated activity; a broad claim that joining makes a firm stronger is not a substitute for that classification. A shared parent can coordinate finance while the activities remain unrelated in production. Conversely, using separate managers does not make stages unrelated if one supplies the other within the same chain. Organisational charts and production relationships answer different questions, so the integration category should follow the economic activities described. The focal firm and production relationship should remain explicit throughout.
